analysis.one_liner: Caps US greenhouse gas emissions with a trading system, giving most pollution permits free to industry.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2007 with six bipartisan cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set a declining nationwide limit on greenhouse gas emissions starting in 2012, with companies buying, selling, or submitting permits for the carbon they emit, or paying a fixed $12-per-ton fee instead. Most permits in the early years would have been given free to coal mines, refineries, power plants, and energy-intensive manufacturers, while a smaller share would have been auctioned to fund clean-energy technology, climate adaptation, and help for low-income households facing higher energy bills.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal mines, oil refineries, natural gas processors, electric generators, and carbon-intensive manufacturers (steel, cement, chemicals, paper) would receive free emissions permits worth significant money each year. Low-income households would gain through a dedicated Energy Assistance Fund for home energy aid and weatherization. Developers of zero- and low-carbon power, cellulosic ethanol, advanced coal with carbon capture, and efficient vehicles would gain access to federal deployment incentives.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Polluting industries and low-income energy users

how_it_helps.text: Sets a hard nationwide cap on greenhouse gas emissions that declines each year, reaching 1990 levels by 2030 and at least 60 percent below 2006 levels by 2050, with the goal of avoiding dangerous climate change [S2] [S3].

Creates an Energy Assistance Fund funded by permit auctions for low-income home energy assistance and weatherization programs, aimed at households 'hardest hit' by the costs of climate policy [S2] [S3].
Requires states to use at least 90 percent of their allowance value to mitigate impacts on low-income energy consumers, promote efficiency, and assist displaced workers [S3].

Funds deployment of zero- or low-carbon power, advanced coal with carbon capture, cellulosic ethanol, and efficient vehicles through a dedicated Energy Technology Deployment Fund financed by the fixed fee payments and permit auctions [S2] [S3].
Gives bonus permits to companies that capture and store carbon underground, rewarding early movers in sequestration [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would bear the carbon cost through higher prices for electricity, gasoline, heating fuel, and goods made by energy-intensive industries, since the entities that burn or sell fossil fuels must hold permits or pay the fee. Electric utilities and fuel distributors would pay for any emissions not covered by their free permits, and taxpayers would fund the technology incentives from allowance revenue.

drawbacks.text: The emissions cap starts very high (6,652 million metric tons in 2012) and declines slowly, only returning to 2006 levels by 2020, and the optional $12-per-ton payment acts as a ceiling on compliance costs, so critics could reasonably call the targets and cost limits too weak to drive deep cuts [S3].

Roughly half of all permits in the first decade (53 percent from 2012 to 2016) would be handed to industry free of charge rather than auctioned, sharply reducing public revenue and transferring valuable assets to the largest emitters [S3].

Households and businesses would pay more for energy and carbon-intensive goods for years while the largest permit value flows to incumbent fossil-fuel companies, a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a genuine first step toward an economy-wide emissions cap with meaningful low-income protections and large clean-energy investments. But its design leaned heavily toward the industries being regulated: free permits for incumbent emitters, a low fixed-fee escape valve, and multibillion-dollar coal and sequestration subsidies. An honest weighing is that the public got a real but modest climate program, while the biggest emitters got most of the permit value and substantial federal support.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee never took the bill up; it sat in committee from July 2007 until the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, without a vote in either chamber.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Bingaman introduced the Low Carbon Economy Act on July 11, 2007, joined by cosponsors from both parties [S1] [S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works the day it was introduced [S5].
Bingaman delivered introductory remarks again on August 2, 2007, but no committee markup, floor vote, or further action followed [S5].
No vote was ever held on the bill in either chamber before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-burning power plants, coal mines, and other fossil fuel emitters were better off, since they continued operating without any federal carbon cost, and no climate pricing law was enacted in that Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Emitters who faced no carbon cost

sides.party_line_note: Four Democrats and three Republicans introduced and cosponsored the bill, but it never reached a vote, so no roll-call exists to show how the broader Senate would have split.

industries.note: The bill would give electric generators 54 percent of the free industry allowances and fund up to 20 gigawatts of advanced coal plants with loan guarantees, grants, or production payments [S3]. Utilities' costs from the carbon cap would largely be offset by free permits while consumers faced higher energy prices [S3].

Coal mines would receive 12 percent of the industry allowance pool, coal facilities could pay a fixed fee instead of cutting emissions, and 25 percent of advanced-coal funding is set aside for lower-rank coals like lignite [S3].

industries.industry: Oil refining and natural gas processing
industries.note: Refineries and gas processors are regulated fuel distributors that must hold allowances, and their costs would flow to consumers at the pump, though they would also receive 7 and 4 percent of the industry allocation free [S3].

These facilities would receive 19 percent of the industry allocation free, distributed partly by workforce size, shielding them from international competition while consumers paid the carbon cost elsewhere [S3].
Farmers could earn sequestration allowances for soil carbon projects, with a standardized certification system, education programs, and federal grants [S3].
The bill funds zero- or low-carbon generation, cellulosic ethanol, and advanced technology vehicle production through reverse auctions and loan guarantees [S3].
